notes.meaning: Job's three friends finally stopped arguing with him because he refused to admit he had done evil. They felt it was useless to keep talking since Job stayed convinced of his own innocence. Even though they became quiet, they were merely silenced rather than persuaded that Job was right.

A young man named Elihu had been listening and became very angry. His family line is given in detail, showing that this story is real history. Elihu was upset with Job for caring more about clearing his own name than defending the justice and honor of God.

Elihu was also angry with the three older friends. They had judged Job to be a wicked man, yet they could not answer his arguments or prove their charges. Elihu felt it was wrong to condemn Job when their own answers had completely failed.

Elihu had kept silent through the whole debate out of respect for his elders. In the ancient world, younger people were expected to wait until older men finished speaking. Elihu showed good manners and patience by waiting his turn.

When Elihu saw that the three friends had completely run out of answers, he could not keep quiet any longer. Their failure to defend God properly stirred up his anger. He felt the time had finally arrived for someone to step in.

Elihu began his speech by admitting that he was much younger than the others. Because of their great age, he had held back out of fear of seeming rude or overly bold. He wanted them to know that his long silence came from humility, not from a lack of thoughts.

Elihu had expected the older men to speak with deep wisdom. Long life usually gives people time to learn, gather experience, and teach others. It was only natural to think that the oldest voices in the room would give the best answers.

Elihu explained that true understanding does not come merely from living many years. It comes from God, who gives human beings the ability to think and grasp the truth. Wisdom is ultimately a gift from the Almighty rather than just the result of old age.

differ.view: Elihu is claiming to speak by the Holy Spirit as a messenger sent with special revelation from God.
Elihu is speaking of the human mind and reasoning ability that God breathes into every person at creation.

notes.meaning: People of high standing or great age do not always have real wisdom. Even the elderly can make mistakes and fail to judge what is right. Because of this, younger people should be heard when they have the truth on their side.

Having shown that wisdom comes from God, Elihu asked the company to give him a hearing. He was ready to state what he knew and offer his own judgment on the debate. He wanted them to weigh his words fairly, even though he was young.

Elihu reminded the friends that he had listened closely while they searched for words. He had not interrupted them, but had given them every chance to build their case. He took the time to understand their reasoning before attempting to answer.

Elihu paid close attention to their arguments, but found that none of them had actually proved Job wrong. They had spoken many words, but none had answered Job's points about his integrity. Since the older men had failed to convince Job, the debate remained unsettled.

Elihu warned the friends not to excuse their failure by saying only God could humble Job. They could not give up and say Job's case was beyond human wisdom just because they were defeated. God had allowed them to fail so they would not boast in their own cleverness.

Elihu pointed out that Job had not directed his complaints against him, so he had no hurt feelings or personal anger. He promised not to repeat the harsh, insulting speeches the three friends had used. He intended to approach the debate in a fresh and fair way.

Elihu looked at the three friends and noted that they sat amazed, having nothing left to say. Their arguments were exhausted, and they had run out of words. Their silence showed that they had lost their ability to carry on the discussion.
Elihu waited to see if any of the three men would speak up. They simply stood there in silence with no further replies. Since they had given up their turn, Elihu felt entirely free to take the floor.

Elihu resolved that he would now share his part in the conversation. Each of the three friends had given their opinion, and now it was his time to declare what he knew. He was eager to present the truth as he saw it.

Elihu felt overflowing with thoughts and arguments after listening for so long. An inner pressure drove him to speak and would not let him remain quiet. He was deeply convinced that he had important truths to deliver.

Elihu compared his inner feelings to fermenting wine trapped in a sealed skin bottle. Without an opening for the gas to escape, a new wineskin will swell until it bursts. His thoughts were stirring inside him so strongly that he felt he would burst if he stayed silent.

Speaking out would give Elihu the relief and room to breathe that he needed. He could no longer hold his thoughts inside without distress. Opening his lips to respond would ease the burden on his mind.

Elihu promised to speak with total fairness, showing favoritism to no one. He would not flatter the wealthy and respected friends, nor soften the truth for suffering Job. He was determined to tell the plain truth without trying to win anyone's approval.

Elihu knew that using empty flattery or dishonest praise was a serious sin against God. He believed that if he lied to please men, his Maker could strike him down in judgment. A healthy reverence for God kept him from being dishonest with people.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The Latin Vulgate tradition translated this verse to mean Elihu did not know how long he would live, rather than fearing sudden judgment for flattery.
